label: def:strong-linearization
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:strong-linearization}
A $dn\times dn$ pencil $L(\lambda)=\lambda X+Y$
is a \emph{linearization} of $P$ if
\[
    U(\lambda)L(\lambda)V(\lambda)
    =\operatorname{diag}\bigl(P(\lambda),I_{(d-1)n}\bigr)
\]
for some unimodular matrix polynomials $U$ and $V$,
that is, matrix polynomials whose determinants are
nonzero constants.

A linearization $L(\lambda)$ is \emph{strong} if
$\operatorname{rev}_1L$ also linearizes
$\operatorname{rev}_dP$, where
\[
    \operatorname{rev}_1L(\lambda)=X+\lambda Y,
    \qquad
    \operatorname{rev}_dP(\lambda)
    =\sum_{k=0}^{d}P_{d-k}\lambda^k.
\]
head: environment

label: prop:one-sided-eigenvector-recovery
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:one-sided-eigenvector-recovery}
Let $\lambda\in\Omega$.
If $L(\lambda)z=0$ and $x=E_{\rm R}z\neq0$, then
$P(\lambda)x=0$.
If $w^*L(\lambda)=0$ and $y=E_{\rm L}^*w\neq0$, then
$y^*P(\lambda)=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Multiplying the first factorization by $z$ gives
\[
    P(\lambda)x
    =H_{\rm R}(\lambda)L(\lambda)z=0.
\]
Multiplying the second by $w^*$ gives
\[
    y^*P(\lambda)
    =w^*L(\lambda)H_{\rm L}(\lambda)=0.
\]
head: environment

label: def:weighted-backward-error
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:weighted-backward-error}
Let $w_0,\ldots,w_d$ be nonnegative weights.
The weighted normwise backward error of a computed eigenpair
$(\lambda,x)$, with $x\neq0$, is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:weighted-backward-error}
    \eta_{P,w}(\lambda,x)
    =
    \inf\left\{
    \varepsilon\geq0:
    \begin{array}{l}
    (P(\lambda)+\Delta P(\lambda))x=0,\\[1mm]
    \|\Delta P_k\|_2\leq\varepsilon w_k,
        \quad k=0,\ldots,d
    \end{array}
    \right\},
\end{equation}
where
\[
    \Delta P(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}\Delta P_k\lambda^k,
    \qquad
    \Delta P_k\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}.
\]
The weights determine how we measure the coefficient
perturbations.
If $w_k=0$, the coefficient $P_k$ cannot change.
head: environment

label: prop:backward-error-residual
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: lem:scaling-reversal-backward-error
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:scaling-reversal-backward-error}
Let $P(\lambda)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}P_k\lambda^k$ be a regular
matrix polynomial.
For $\gamma>0$ and
$\delta\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$, define
\[
    Q(t)=\delta P(\gamma t),
    \qquad
    R(t)=\operatorname{rev}_dP(t)
        =\sum_{k=0}^{d}P_{d-k}t^k.
\]
For any matrix polynomial $F(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}F_kt^k$,
write
\[
    S_F(r)=\sum_{k=0}^{d}\|F_k\|_2r^k,
    \qquad r\geq0,
\]
with $r^0=1$, including at $r=0$.
Then
\begin{align}
    S_Q(r)&=|\delta|S_P(\gamma r),
    &&r\geq0,
    \label{eq:scaled-polynomial-weight}\\
    S_R(r)&=r^dS_P(r^{-1}),
    &&r>0.
    \label{eq:reversed-polynomial-weight}
\end{align}
Let $\eta_F^{\rm R}$ and $\eta_F^{\rm L}$ denote the
right and left normwise backward errors with weights
$\|F_k\|_2$.
For nonzero vectors $x,y\in\mathbb C^n$,
\begin{align}
    \eta_Q^{\rm R}(x,t)
    &=\eta_P^{\rm R}(x,\gamma t),
    &
    \eta_Q^{\rm L}(y,t)
    &=\eta_P^{\rm L}(y,\gamma t),
    &&t\in\mathbb C,
    \label{eq:scaled-polynomial-backward-error}\\
    \eta_R^{\rm R}(x,t)
    &=\eta_P^{\rm R}(x,t^{-1}),
    &
    \eta_R^{\rm L}(y,t)
    &=\eta_P^{\rm L}(y,t^{-1}),
    &&t\neq0.
    \label{eq:reversed-polynomial-backward-error}
\end{align}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since
\[
    \|\delta\gamma^kP_k\|_2
    =|\delta|\gamma^k\|P_k\|_2,
\]
summing over $k$ gives
\eqref{eq:scaled-polynomial-weight}.
Moreover,
\[
    Q(t)x=\delta P(\gamma t)x,
    \qquad
    y^*Q(t)=\delta y^*P(\gamma t).
\]
Thus, scaling multiplies each residual norm and its
backward-error denominator by the same factor $|\delta|$.

For reversal, reindexing gives
\[
    S_R(r)
    =\sum_{k=0}^{d}\|P_{d-k}\|_2r^k
    =r^dS_P(r^{-1}).
\]
The identity $R(t)=t^dP(t^{-1})$ shows that both the residual norm and its denominator are multiplied by $|t|^d$.
The backward-error identities follow.
head: environment

label: lem:linearization-scaling-reversal
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:linearization-scaling-reversal}
Let $L(\lambda)$ be a linearization of a matrix
polynomial $P(\lambda)$ of grade $d$.
For $\gamma>0$ and nonzero scalars $\delta,\kappa$,
define
\[
    Q(t)=\delta P(\gamma t),
    \qquad
    M(t)=\kappa L(\gamma t).
\]
Then $M$ is a linearization of $Q$.
If $L$ is strong, then $M$ is strong, and
$\operatorname{rev}_1L$ is a strong linearization
of $\operatorname{rev}_dP$.
head: environment
name: Scaling and reversal of linearizations

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose
\[
    A(\lambda)L(\lambda)B(\lambda)
    =\operatorname{diag}(P(\lambda),I_{(d-1)n}),
\]
where $A$ and $B$ are unimodular.
Substituting $\lambda=\gamma t$ preserves
unimodularity. Multiplication by the constant
invertible matrix
\[
    \operatorname{diag}
    \bigl((\delta/\kappa)I_n,
          \kappa^{-1}I_{(d-1)n}\bigr)
\]
then gives a unimodular equivalence between $M$
and $\operatorname{diag}(Q,I_{(d-1)n})$.

If $L$ is strong, apply the same argument to
$\operatorname{rev}_1L$ and
$\operatorname{rev}_dP$, using
\[
    \operatorname{rev}_1M(t)
    =\kappa\gamma\,
      \operatorname{rev}_1L(t/\gamma),
    \qquad
    \operatorname{rev}_dQ(t)
    =\delta\gamma^d\,
      \operatorname{rev}_dP(t/\gamma).
\]
Thus $M$ is strong.

Finally, $\operatorname{rev}_1L$ linearizes
$\operatorname{rev}_dP$ by the strong property.
Reversing both again gives $L$ and $P$, so this
linearization is also strong.

label: prop:backward-error-transfer
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: def:backward-error-growth-factors
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:backward-error-growth-factors}
For the chosen one-sided factorizations, define the
right and left residual amplification factors by
\[
    g_{\rm R}(\lambda)
    =
    \frac{W_L(|\lambda|)\|H_{\rm R}(\lambda)\|_2}
         {S_P(|\lambda|)},
    \qquad
    g_{\rm L}(\lambda)
    =
    \frac{W_L(|\lambda|)\|H_{\rm L}(\lambda)\|_2}
         {S_P(|\lambda|)}.
\]
For pencil vectors with nonzero selected blocks,
define the recovery norm ratios by
\[
    \rho_{\rm R}(z)
    =\frac{\|z\|_2}{\|E_{\rm R}z\|_2},
    \qquad
    \rho_{\rm L}(w)
    =\frac{\|w\|_2}{\|E_{\rm L}^*w\|_2}.
\]
The corresponding backward-error growth factors are
the products
\[
    \Gamma_{\rm R}(\lambda,z)
    =g_{\rm R}(\lambda)\rho_{\rm R}(z),
    \qquad
    \Gamma_{\rm L}(\lambda,w)
    =g_{\rm L}(\lambda)\rho_{\rm L}(w).
\]

label: prop:tropical-dominance
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:tropical-dominance}
For an interior index $j$ with $a_j>0$,
\[
    I_j=
    \begin{cases}
        [\ell_j,h_j],&\ell_j\leq h_j,\\
        \varnothing,&\ell_j>h_j.
    \end{cases}
\]
The upper convex hull gives the following description:
\begin{enumerate}
    \par\hangindent 40\p@ If $j=v_i$ is an interior hull vertex, then
    \[
        I_j=[\alpha_i,\alpha_{i+1}].
    \]
    \par\hangindent 40\p@ If $(j,\log a_j)$ lies in the relative interior of the hull segment associated with $\alpha_i$, then
    \[
        I_j=\{\alpha_i\}.
    \]
    \par\hangindent 40\p@ If $(j,\log a_j)$ lies strictly below the
    upper hull, then $I_j=\varnothing$.
\end{enumerate}
The endpoint intervals are
\[
    I_0=(0,\alpha_1],
    \qquad
    I_d=[\alpha_s,\infty).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k<j$ with $a_k>0$,
\[
    a_kr^k\leq a_jr^j
    \quad\text{ if and only if }\quad
    r\geq\left(\frac{a_k}{a_j}\right)^{1/(j-k)}.
\]
For $k>j$ with $a_k>0$,
\[
    a_kr^k\leq a_jr^j
    \quad\text{ if and only if }\quad
    r\leq\left(\frac{a_j}{a_k}\right)^{1/(k-j)}.
\]
Terms with $a_k=0$ impose no restriction.
Intersecting these inequalities gives the formula for $I_j$.

For an interior hull vertex $v_i$, the line
$\log a_{v_i}+v_i u$ attains the maximum defining
$\phi_P(u)$ precisely between the consecutive breakpoints
$\log\alpha_i$ and $\log\alpha_{i+1}$, including both
endpoints. This gives $I_{v_i}=[\alpha_i,\alpha_{i+1}]$.

A coefficient point inside a hull segment attains the
maximum only at the breakpoint associated with that
segment. A point strictly below the hull never attains
the maximum. Finally, the terms of degree zero and $d$
dominate before the first breakpoint and after the last,
respectively, giving the endpoint intervals.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
For the degree-five example in Figure~\ref{fig:tropical-degree-five}, the coefficient norms are
\[
    (a_0,\ldots,a_5)=(1,10,10^4,10^5,10^6,10^4),
\]
and the tropical roots are
\[
    \alpha_1=10^{-2},\qquad
    \alpha_2=10^{-1},\qquad
    \alpha_3=10^2.
\]
The hull vertices have indices $0,2,4,5$, so their dominance intervals are
\[
    I_0=(0,10^{-2}],\qquad
    I_2=[10^{-2},10^{-1}],\qquad
    I_4=[10^{-1},10^2],\qquad
    I_5=[10^2,\infty).
\]
The point at index $1$ lies below the hull, giving $I_1=\varnothing$. 
The point at index $3$ lies inside the hull segment joining indices $2$ and $4$, giving
\[
    I_3=\{10^{-1}\}.
\]
At $r=10^{-1}$, the three terms $a_2r^2$, $a_3r^3$, and $a_4r^4$ all attain $T_P(r)$.
head: environment

label: cor:dominance-covering
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:dominance-covering}
The dominance intervals associated with the upper hull vertices cover all positive radii:
\[
    \bigcup_{i=0}^{s} I_{v_i}=(0,\infty).
\]
Consequently,
\[
    \bigcup_{i=0}^{s}\mathcal D_{v_i}
    =\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}.
\]
With the convention that $0\in\mathcal D_0$, these
regions cover the whole complex plane.

No other coefficient indices are needed for this
covering.
Points below the hull have empty dominance intervals, and points inside hull segments have singleton intervals already contained in those of
the adjacent hull vertices.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The vertex intervals are
\[
    I_{v_0}=(0,\alpha_1],\qquad
    I_{v_i}=[\alpha_i,\alpha_{i+1}]
    \quad(1\leq i\leq s-1),\qquad
    I_{v_s}=[\alpha_s,\infty).
\]
Their union is $(0,\infty)$.
A point inside the $i$th hull segment has dominance interval $\{\alpha_i\}$, which lies in both $I_{v_{i-1}}$ and $I_{v_i}$.
head: environment

label: lem:tropical-coefficient-decay
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tropical-coefficient-decay}
Suppose $s\geq2$, and let $j=v_i$ be an interior hull vertex, with $1\leq i\leq s-1$.
Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:tropical-coefficient-decay}
    \|Q_{j,j}\|_2=1,
    \qquad
    \|Q_{j,k}\|_2\leq U_j^{-|k-j|},
    \qquad 0\leq k\leq d.
\end{equation}
Moreover, for $U_j^{-1}\leq r\leq U_j$,
\[
    T_{Q_j}(r)=r^j,
    \qquad
    r^j\leq S_{Q_j}(r)\leq(d+1)r^j.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $k<j$, dominance at $\ell_j$ gives
\[
    a_k\ell_j^k\leq a_j\ell_j^j.
\]
Consequently,
\[
    \|Q_{j,k}\|_2
    =\frac{a_k}{a_j}\gamma_j^{k-j}
    \leq
    \left(\frac{\ell_j}{\gamma_j}\right)^{j-k}
    =U_j^{-(j-k)}.
\]
For $k>j$, dominance at $h_j$ similarly gives
\[
    \|Q_{j,k}\|_2
    \leq
    \left(\frac{\gamma_j}{h_j}\right)^{k-j}
    =U_j^{-(k-j)}.
\]
These inequalities also hold when $a_k=0$.
For $k=j$, the normalization gives
$\|Q_{j,j}\|_2=1$.

If $U_j^{-1}\leq r\leq U_j$, then
$\gamma_jr\in I_j$. Therefore
\[
    T_{Q_j}(r)
    =\frac{T_P(\gamma_jr)}{a_j\gamma_j^j}
    =r^j.
\]
The bounds for $S_{Q_j}(r)$ follow from
\eqref{eq:tropical-sum-comparison}.

title: Example
head: environment

label: prop:interior-strong-linearization
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:interior-strong-linearization}
The pencil $S_{j,U}$ is a strong linearization of $Q$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Multiply block column $h$ by $U^{-\max\{h-j,0\}}$, for $0\leq h\leq d-1$.
The body row becomes
\[
    [Q_{d-1}+tQ_d,\ Q_{d-2},\ldots,Q_0].
\]
For each auxiliary row indexed by $h$, multiply by $-U^{h-j}$ if $h>j$, and by $U$ if $h\leq j$.
Its two nonzero blocks then become $[-I_n,tI_n]$.

These constant invertible row and column scalings transform $S_{j,U}$ into the Frobenius companion pencil $C_Q$. Since $C_Q$ is a strong linearization of $Q$, so is $S_{j,U}$.
head: environment

label: ex:degree-five-pencils
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:degree-five-pencils}
Let
\[
    Q(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{5}Q_kt^k
\]
be regular, and fix $U\geq1$.

For $j=2$, we have $p=q=2$, and the construction gives
\[
    S_{2,U}(t)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        U^2(Q_4+tQ_5)&UQ_3&Q_2&Q_1&Q_0\\
        I_n&-\frac{t}{U}I_n&0&0&0\\
        0&I_n&-\frac{t}{U}I_n&0&0\\
        0&0&-\frac1U I_n&\frac{t}{U}I_n&0\\
        0&0&0&-\frac1U I_n&\frac{t}{U}I_n
    \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Both types of auxiliary row appear twice.

For $j=4$, we have $p=0$ and $q=4$, giving
\[
    S_{4,U}(t)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        Q_4+tQ_5&Q_3&Q_2&Q_1&Q_0\\
        -\frac1U I_n&\frac{t}{U}I_n&0&0&0\\
        0&-\frac1U I_n&\frac{t}{U}I_n&0&0\\
        0&0&-\frac1U I_n&\frac{t}{U}I_n&0\\
        0&0&0&-\frac1U I_n&\frac{t}{U}I_n
    \end{bmatrix}.
\]
Here every auxiliary row has blocks $-U^{-1}I_n$ and $(t/U)I_n$.

Both pencils are strong linearizations of the same polynomial $Q$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:interior-strong-linearization}.
head: environment
name: Degree-five pencils

label: prop:interior-one-sided-factorizations
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:interior-one-sided-factorizations}
For $t\neq0$ and $0\leq h\leq d-1$, there are matrix
functions $F_h(t)$ and $G_h(t)$ such that
\begin{align}
\label{eq:interior-all-right-factorizations}
    G_h(t)S(t)&=\beta_h(t)Q(t)E_h^*,\\
\label{eq:interior-all-left-factorizations}
    S(t)F_h(t)&=E_{\rm b}\,\beta_h(t)Q(t),
\end{align}
where
\[
    \beta_h(t)=U^{\max\{h-j,0\}}t^{-h}.
\]
They satisfy
\[
    E_h^*F_h(t)=I_n,
    \qquad
    G_h(t)E_{\rm b}=I_n.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $t\neq0$, define
\[
    c_k(t)=
    \begin{cases}
        (t/U)^{k-j}, & k>j,\\
        t^{k-j}, & k\leq j.
    \end{cases}
\]
Then
\[
    F_h(t)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        \dfrac{c_{d-1}(t)}{c_h(t)}I_n\\
        \vdots\\
        \dfrac{c_0(t)}{c_h(t)}I_n
    \end{bmatrix}
    =
    U^{\max\{h-j,0\}}t^{j-h}
    \begin{bmatrix}
        (t/U)^{d-1-j}I_n\\
        \vdots\\
        (t/U)I_n\\
        I_n\\
        t^{-1}I_n\\
        \vdots\\
        t^{-j}I_n
    \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The blocks above $I_n$ are absent when $j=d-1$.
Equivalently, the block indexed by $k$ is
\[
    (F_h(t))_k
    =
    U^{\max\{h-j,0\}-\max\{k-j,0\}}
    t^{k-h}I_n,
    \qquad 0\leq k\leq d-1.
\]



The blocks of $F_h(t)$ satisfy the auxiliary equations,
and its block indexed by $h$ is $I_n$. Hence
\[
    E_h^*F_h(t)=I_n.
\]
Substitution into the body row gives
\[
    S(t)F_h(t)
    =E_{\rm b}\frac{t^{-j}}{c_h(t)}Q(t)
    =E_{\rm b}\,\beta_h(t)Q(t),
\]
where
\[
    \beta_h(t)
    =\frac{t^{-j}}{c_h(t)}
    =U^{\max\{h-j,0\}}t^{-h}.
\]

For the other factorization, let $B_h(t)$ be the
matrix obtained by deleting column $h$ from the
auxiliary rows, and let $C_h(t)$ be the body row
with the same column deleted.

The matrix $B_h(t)$ is invertible. Indeed, a vector
in its kernel extends to an auxiliary solution with
block $h$ equal to zero. The auxiliary equations then
force every block to vanish.

Set
\[
    G_h(t)=[I_n,-C_h(t)B_h(t)^{-1}].
\]
Then $G_h(t)S(t)$ vanishes in every column except $h$.
Since $E_h^*F_h(t)=I_n$, its remaining block is
\[
    G_h(t)S(t)F_h(t)=\beta_h(t)Q(t).
\]
This proves the first factorization.
The first block of $G_h(t)$ is $I_n$, giving
$G_h(t)E_{\rm b}=I_n$.
head: environment

label: prop:interior-eigenvector-recovery
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{prop:interior-eigenvector-recovery}
Let $t\neq0$. For every nonzero right pencil eigenvector
$v$, each block
\[
    x=E_h^*v=v_h,\qquad 0\leq h\leq d-1,
\]
is a nonzero right eigenvector of $Q$.
For every nonzero left pencil eigenvector $w$, the
body block
\[
    y^*=w^*E_{\rm b}
\]
is a nonzero left eigenvector of $Q$.
Moreover,
\[
    v=F_h(t)x,\qquad w^*=y^*G_h(t).
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The factorizations give $Q(t)x=0$ and $y^*Q(t)=0$,
since $\beta_h(t)\neq0$.

The right auxiliary equations give $v=F_h(t)x$,
so $x=0$ would force $v=0$.
On the left, the equations in the columns other than
$h$ give
\[
    w^*=y^*[I_n,-C_h(t)B_h(t)^{-1}]
        =y^*G_h(t).
\]
Thus $y=0$ would force $w=0$.
head: environment

label: prop:half-annulus-residual-amplification
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:half-annulus-residual-amplification}
For every interior hull vertex $j$, the pencils
$L_j^+$ and $L_j^-$, with the recovery positions in
Table~\ref{tab:recovery-positions}, satisfy
\[
    g_{\rm R}^{\pm}(\lambda)\leq A_dB_d,
    \qquad
    g_{\rm L}^{\pm}(\lambda)\leq A_d\sqrt d
\]
on $\mathcal R_j^\pm$, respectively, where
\[
    A_d=\sqrt d+3,
    \qquad
    B_d=
    \left(1+\frac{(d-1)d(2d-1)}6\right)^{1/2}.
\]
The bounds include the boundaries and depend only on $d$.
head: environment
name: Residual amplification on the half annuli

label: eq:interior-coefficient-assumptions
title: Proof
body_md:
We first establish the bounds for $S=S_{j,U}$ and a
polynomial $Q$ satisfying
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:interior-coefficient-assumptions}
    \|Q_j\|_2=1,
    \qquad
    \|Q_k\|_2\leq U^{-|k-j|},
    \qquad 0\leq k\leq d.
\end{equation}
Use right recovery from position $d-j$ and left
recovery from position $1$.

Write $r=|t|$ and $S(t)=tX+Y$, with $1\leq r\leq U$.
The $t$-dependent body block and auxiliary part each
have norm at most $U^{-1}$, so $\|X\|_2\leq2/U$.
Every constant body block has norm at most one,
and the constant auxiliary part has norm at most one.
Hence $\|Y\|_2\leq\sqrt d+1$, giving
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:interior-pencil-weight-bound}
    W_S(r)\leq 2r/U+\sqrt d+1\leq A_d.
\end{equation}
Also, $S_Q(r)\geq r^j$.

The one-sided factorizations for these recovery blocks
give
\[
    g_{\rm R}(t)
    =\frac{W_S(r)r^j\|G_j(t)\|_2}{S_Q(r)},
    \qquad
    g_{\rm L}(t)
    =\frac{W_S(r)r^j\|F_j(t)\|_2}{S_Q(r)}.
\]
Every scalar block of $F_j(t)$ has modulus at most
one on this region, so $\|F_j(t)\|_2\leq\sqrt d$.

To bound $G_j$, write
\[
    G_j(t)=[I_n,G_{j,d-1}(t),\ldots,G_{j,1}(t)],
\]
where $G_{j,q}$ corresponds to auxiliary row $q$.
Cancellation of the columns other than $j$ gives
\[
    G_{j,q}(t)
    =
    \begin{cases}
        \displaystyle
        -U\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}Q_kt^{-(q-k)},
        &1\leq q\leq j,\\[6pt]
        \displaystyle
        -\sum_{k=q}^{d-1}
          U^{k-j}Q_k(t/U)^{k-q}
        -tU^{d-1-j}Q_d(t/U)^{d-1-q},
        &j<q\leq d-1.
    \end{cases}
\]
Each summand has norm at most one. For the first case,
this follows from
\[
    U\|Q_k\|_2r^{-(q-k)}
    \leq U^{1-(j-k)}r^{-(q-k)}\leq1.
\]
For the second case, each term in the sum has norm
at most $(r/U)^{k-q}\leq1$. The final term satisfies
\[
    \bigl\|tU^{d-1-j}Q_d(t/U)^{d-1-q}\bigr\|_2
    \leq
    rU^{-1}(r/U)^{d-1-q}
    =(r/U)^{d-q}\leq1.
\]
Therefore,
\[
    \|G_{j,q}(t)\|_2
    \leq
    \begin{cases}
        q, & q\leq j,\\
        d-q+1, & q>j.
    \end{cases}
\]
Consequently,
\[
    \|G_j(t)\|_2^2
    \leq
    1+\sum_{q=1}^{j}q^2
      +\sum_{q=j+1}^{d-1}(d-q+1)^2
    \leq
    1+\sum_{q=1}^{d-1}q^2
    =B_d^2,
\]
where the second inequality follows from
\[
    \sum_{q=1}^{d-1}q^2
    -\sum_{q=1}^{j}q^2
    -\sum_{q=j+1}^{d-1}(d-q+1)^2
    =(j-1)(d-j-1)(d+1)\geq0.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:interior-pencil-weight-bound}
and $S_Q(r)\geq r^j$, these estimates prove the
direct bounds.

For $L_j^+$, apply these bounds to $Q_j$ with
$t=\lambda/\gamma_j$.
For $L_j^-$, apply them to $\widetilde Q_j$ with
dominant index $d-j$ and $s=\gamma_j/\lambda$.
The respective assigned regions give
$1\leq|t|\leq U_j$ and $1\leq|s|\leq U_j$.
Scaling and reversal preserve the residual amplification
factors, so the same bounds hold in the original variable.
head: environment

label: prop:endpoint-extension
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:endpoint-extension}
For the last interior hull vertex $j=v_{s-1}$,
the pencil $L_j^+$ extends to
\[
    |\lambda|\geq\gamma_j
    =\sqrt{\alpha_{s-1}\alpha_s}.
\]
Use right recovery from position $d-j$ for
$\gamma_j\leq|\lambda|\leq\alpha_s$, and from
position $1$ for $|\lambda|\geq\alpha_s$.

For the first interior hull vertex $j=v_1$,
the pencil $L_j^-$ extends to
\[
    0<|\lambda|\leq\gamma_j
    =\sqrt{\alpha_1\alpha_2}.
\]
Use right recovery from position $j$ for
$\alpha_1\leq|\lambda|\leq\gamma_j$, and from
position $1$ for $0<|\lambda|\leq\alpha_1$.

With left recovery from position $1$ in both cases,
the residual amplification factors satisfy
\[
    g_{\rm R}(\lambda)\leq A_dB_d,
    \qquad
    g_{\rm L}(\lambda)\leq A_d\sqrt d
\]
on the extended regions, with the same constants
as in Proposition~\ref{prop:half-annulus-residual-amplification}.
At an endpoint root, either adjacent right recovery
rule may be used.
head: environment
name: Endpoint extension

title: Proof
body_md:
We first extend the last upper-half pencil.
Write
\[
    j=v_{s-1},\qquad
    Q=Q_j,\qquad U=U_j,\qquad
    t=\lambda/\gamma_j,\qquad r=|t|.
\]
The existing bounds cover $1\leq r\leq U$.
Since $\alpha_s=\gamma_jU$, it remains to consider
$r\geq U$.

The last hull segment joins $j$ to $d$, so
\[
    a_j\alpha_s^j=a_d\alpha_s^d.
\]
Consequently,
\[
    \|Q_d\|_2
    =\frac{a_d}{a_j}\gamma_j^{d-j}
    =U^{-(d-j)},
    \qquad
    S_Q(r)\geq U^{-(d-j)}r^d.
\]

Use extraction from block index $d-1$, which is
position $1$. Its one-sided factorizations are
\[
    G_{d-1}(t)S(t)
    =\beta_{d-1}(t)Q(t)E_{d-1}^*,
\]
and
\[
    S(t)F_{d-1}(t)
    =E_{\rm b}\,\beta_{d-1}(t)Q(t),
\]
where
\[
    \beta_{d-1}(t)=U^{d-1-j}t^{-(d-1)}.
\]
The coefficient estimates for the pencil give
\[
    W_S(r)\leq 2r/U+\sqrt d+1
             \leq A_d\,r/U,
    \qquad r\geq U.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:endpoint-weight-bound}
    \frac{W_S(r)}
         {|\beta_{d-1}(t)|S_Q(r)}
    \leq A_d.
\end{equation}

The blocks of $F_{d-1}$ are
\[
    (F_{d-1}(t))_k=
    \begin{cases}
        (t/U)^{k-(d-1)}I_n,&k\geq j,\\
        (t/U)^{j-(d-1)}t^{k-j}I_n,&k<j.
    \end{cases}
\]
Their scalar factors have modulus at most one for
$r\geq U\geq1$. Hence
\[
    \|F_{d-1}(t)\|_2\leq\sqrt d.
\]

To bound the complementary multiplier, write
\[
    G_{d-1}(t)
    =[I_n,H_{d-1}(t),\ldots,H_1(t)].
\]
Cancellation of the columns below index $j$ gives
\[
    H_q(t)
    =-U\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}Q_kt^{-(q-k)},
    \qquad 1\leq q\leq j.
\]
Each summand has norm at most one, so
$\|H_q(t)\|_2\leq q$.

If $j<d-1$, cancellation of column $j$ gives
\[
    H_{j+1}(t)=\frac{U}{t}Q_j-\frac1t H_j(t).
\]
Thus $\|H_{j+1}(t)\|_2\leq j+1$.
The remaining cancellation equations are
\[
    H_{q+1}(t)
    =\frac{U}{t}\bigl(U^{q-j}Q_q+H_q(t)\bigr),
    \qquad j<q<d-1.
\]
Since $U/r\leq1$ and
$\|U^{q-j}Q_q\|_2\leq1$, induction gives
$\|H_q(t)\|_2\leq q$ for every $q$.
Therefore
\[
    \|G_{d-1}(t)\|_2^2
    \leq1+\sum_{q=1}^{d-1}q^2=B_d^2.
\]
Combining these multiplier bounds with
\eqref{eq:endpoint-weight-bound} proves
\[
    g_{\rm R}(t)\leq A_dB_d,
    \qquad
    g_{\rm L}(t)\leq A_d\sqrt d
\]
for $r\geq U$. Scaling transfers the bounds to
$|\lambda|\geq\alpha_s$.

Finally, apply this argument to the reversed polynomial.
Its last interior hull vertex corresponds to $v_1$
for $P$, and its last tropical root corresponds to
$\alpha_1$. Reversal transfers the extension to
$0<|\lambda|\leq\alpha_1$, with right recovery from
position $1$. Together with the original lower-half
bounds, this proves the second extension.
head: environment

label: prop:single-root-residual-amplification
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:single-root-residual-amplification}
With these recovery rules, the single pencil
$L_\alpha$ covers $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ and satisfies
\[
    g_{\rm R}(\lambda)\leq A_d\widehat B_d,
    \qquad
    g_{\rm L}(\lambda)\leq A_d\sqrt d,
\]
where
\[
    A_d=\sqrt d+3,
    \qquad
    \widehat B_d=
    \left(\frac{d(d+1)(2d+1)}6\right)^{1/2}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Work in the scaled variable $t=\lambda/\alpha$,
and write $r=|t|$.
The coefficient bounds give
\[
    S_B(r)\geq1+r^d,
    \qquad
    W_{C_B}(r)\leq2r+\sqrt d+1.
\]
Consequently,
\[
    W_{C_B}(r)\leq
    \begin{cases}
        A_d,&r\leq1,\\
        A_dr,&r\geq1.
    \end{cases}
\]

For $0<r\leq1$, extract the last right block.
The one-sided factorizations have scalar multiplier
$\beta(t)=1$, with
\[
    F(t)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        t^{d-1}I_n\\
        \vdots\\
        I_n
    \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The complementary block row is
\[
    G(t)=[I_n,H_{d-1}(t),\ldots,H_1(t)],
    \qquad
    H_q(t)=\sum_{k=q}^{d}B_kt^{k-q}.
\]
Hence
\[
    \|F(t)\|_2\leq\sqrt d,
    \qquad
    \|H_q(t)\|_2\leq d-q+1,
\]
and
\[
    \|G(t)\|_2^2
    \leq1+\sum_{q=1}^{d-1}(d-q+1)^2
    =\widehat B_d^2.
\]
Since $S_B(r)\geq1$, the claimed bounds follow
on this region.

For $r\geq1$, extract the first right block.
Now $\beta(t)=t^{-(d-1)}$, and
\[
    F(t)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        I_n\\
        t^{-1}I_n\\
        \vdots\\
        t^{-(d-1)}I_n
    \end{bmatrix},
    \qquad
    H_q(t)=-\sum_{k=0}^{q-1}B_kt^{-(q-k)}.
\]
Thus $\|F(t)\|_2\leq\sqrt d$ and
$\|H_q(t)\|_2\leq q$, giving
$\|G(t)\|_2\leq\widehat B_d$.
Moreover,
\[
    \frac{W_{C_B}(r)}
         {|\beta(t)|S_B(r)}
    \leq
    \frac{A_dr\,r^{d-1}}{r^d}
    =A_d.
\]
This proves the bounds for $r\geq1$.
Scaling transfers both bounds to the original variable.
head: environment

label: thm:linearization-covering
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:linearization-covering}
Let $P$ be regular of degree $d\geq2$, with $a_0,a_d>0$,
and let $s$ be the number of distinct tropical roots.
The constructions above give strong linearizations
whose assigned regions cover $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$.
The number of pencils is
\[
    N(s)=
    \begin{cases}
        1,&s=1,\\
        2(s-1),&s\geq2.
    \end{cases}
\]
head: environment
name: Linearization covering

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $s\geq2$. There are $s-1$ interior hull
vertices. The two pencils for vertex $v_i$ cover
the radial intervals
\[
    [\alpha_i,\gamma_{v_i}]
    \quad\text{and}\quad
    [\gamma_{v_i},\alpha_{i+1}].
\]
Their union over all interior vertices is
$[\alpha_1,\alpha_s]$.

The first lower-half pencil extends to
$(0,\gamma_{v_1}]$, and the last upper-half pencil
extends to $[\gamma_{v_{s-1}},\infty)$.
Hence the $2(s-1)$ pencils cover every positive radius.

If $s=1$, the two recovery regions of $L_\alpha$
cover every positive radius.
All pencils are strong linearizations by the
construction, scaling, and reversal arguments above.
head: environment

label: ex:degree-five-pencils
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:degree-five-pencils}

Consider again the coefficient norms
\[
    (a_0,\ldots,a_5)=(1,10,10^4,10^5,10^6,10^4).
\]
The tropical roots are
\[
    \alpha_1=10^{-2},\qquad
    \alpha_2=10^{-1},\qquad
    \alpha_3=10^2,
\]
and the interior hull vertices are $2$ and $4$.
Their midpoint scales and width parameters are
\[
    \gamma_2=10^{-3/2},\qquad U_2=10^{1/2},
    \qquad
    \gamma_4=10^{1/2},\qquad U_4=10^{3/2}.
\]

Write
\[
    A_k=Q_{2,k},\qquad B_k=Q_{4,k},
    \qquad u=U_2,\qquad v=U_4.
\]
For $j=2$, the direct pencil is
\[
    S_2^+(t)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        u^2(A_4+tA_5)&uA_3&A_2&A_1&A_0\\
        I_n&-\frac{t}{u}I_n&0&0&0\\
        0&I_n&-\frac{t}{u}I_n&0&0\\
        0&0&-\frac1u I_n&\frac{t}{u}I_n&0\\
        0&0&0&-\frac1u I_n&\frac{t}{u}I_n
    \end{bmatrix}.
\]
For $j=4$, we have
\[
    S_4^+(t)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        B_4+tB_5&B_3&B_2&B_1&B_0\\
        -\frac1v I_n&\frac{t}{v}I_n&0&0&0\\
        0&-\frac1v I_n&\frac{t}{v}I_n&0&0\\
        0&0&-\frac1v I_n&\frac{t}{v}I_n&0\\
        0&0&0&-\frac1v I_n&\frac{t}{v}I_n
    \end{bmatrix}.
\]

Reversal changes the dominant indices to $3$ and $1$,
respectively. The corresponding pencils are
\[
    \widetilde S_2(s)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        u(A_1+sA_0)&A_2&A_3&A_4&A_5\\
        I_n&-\frac{s}{u}I_n&0&0&0\\
        0&-\frac1u I_n&\frac{s}{u}I_n&0&0\\
        0&0&-\frac1u I_n&\frac{s}{u}I_n&0\\
        0&0&0&-\frac1u I_n&\frac{s}{u}I_n
    \end{bmatrix}
\]
and
\[
    \widetilde S_4(s)=
    \begin{bmatrix}
        v^3(B_1+sB_0)&v^2B_2&vB_3&B_4&B_5\\
        I_n&-\frac{s}{v}I_n&0&0&0\\
        0&I_n&-\frac{s}{v}I_n&0&0\\
        0&0&I_n&-\frac{s}{v}I_n&0\\
        0&0&0&-\frac1v I_n&\frac{s}{v}I_n
    \end{bmatrix}.
\]
The four original-variable pencils are
\[
    L_j^+(\lambda)=S_j^+(\lambda/\gamma_j),
    \qquad
    L_j^-(\lambda)
    =\frac{\lambda}{\gamma_j}
       \widetilde S_j(\gamma_j/\lambda),
    \qquad j\in\{2,4\}.
\]

After the endpoint extensions, the assigned radii and
right recovery positions are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
    \text{Pencil}&\text{Assigned radii}
        &\text{Right recovery position}\\ \hline
    L_2^-&(0,10^{-3/2}]
        &1\text{ below }10^{-2};
         \ 2\text{ above }10^{-2}\\
    L_2^+&[10^{-3/2},10^{-1}]&3\\
    L_4^-&[10^{-1},10^{1/2}]&4\\
    L_4^+&[10^{1/2},\infty)&1
\end{array}
\]
Positions are numbered from $1$ to $5$ in the displayed
companion ordering. At a recovery boundary, either
adjacent rule may be used.

For $L_4^+$, the dominant block is already the first
block, so its endpoint extension does not change the
recovery position. Left recovery uses the body block
for all four pencils.

Thus, four pencils cover all nonzero radii, compared
with the degree-based bound of eight.
head: environment
name: The degree-five construction

label: prop:exact-interior-ratios
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:exact-interior-ratios}
Let $1\leq|t|\leq U$.
For every nonzero right and left eigenvector of
$S_{j,U}(t)$, the selected blocks are nonzero and
\[
    \rho_{\rm R}(v)=f_{j,U}(|t|),
    \qquad
    1\leq\rho_{\rm R}(v)\leq\sqrt d,
\]
and
\[
    1\leq\rho_{\rm L}(w)\leq B_d.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Corollary~\ref{prop:interior-eigenvector-recovery}
gives $x,y\neq0$ and
\[
    v=F_j(t)x,
    \qquad
    w^*=y^*G_j(t).
\]
Adding the squared right block norms gives
\[
    \|v\|_2^2
    =
    \left(
        \sum_{k=0}^{p}(|t|/U)^{2k}
        +\sum_{k=1}^{j}|t|^{-2k}
    \right)\|x\|_2^2.
\]
The sum contains $d$ terms, each at most one,
and includes a term equal to one.
This proves the right statement.

The multiplier estimate established in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:half-annulus-residual-amplification}
gives $\|G_j(t)\|_2\leq B_d$.
Hence
\[
    \|w\|_2=\|y^*G_j(t)\|_2\leq B_d\|y\|_2.
\]
Block extraction gives the lower bound.
head: environment

label: prop:exact-endpoint-ratios
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:exact-endpoint-ratios}
For the large endpoint extension, with
$j=v_{s-1}$ and $|\lambda|\geq\alpha_s$,
the selected blocks are nonzero and
\[
    \rho_{\rm R}(v)
    =e_{j,U_j}(|\lambda|/\gamma_j)
    \leq\sqrt d,
    \qquad
    \rho_{\rm L}(w)\leq B_d.
\]
For the small endpoint extension, with
$j=v_1$ and $0<|\lambda|\leq\alpha_1$,
they are nonzero and
\[
    \rho_{\rm R}(v)
    =e_{d-j,U_j}(\gamma_j/|\lambda|)
    \leq\sqrt d,
    \qquad
    \rho_{\rm L}(w)\leq B_d.
\]
All four ratios are at least one.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the large endpoint, set
$t=\lambda/\gamma_j$ and $r=|t|$.
Since $\alpha_s=\gamma_jU_j$, we have $r\geq U_j$.
The block formulas give
\[
    \|v\|_2^2
    =
    \left(
        \sum_{k=0}^{p}(U_j/r)^{2k}
        +U_j^{2p}\sum_{k=1}^{j}r^{-2(p+k)}
    \right)\|x\|_2^2.
\]
Each of the $d$ terms is at most one:
in the second sum,
\[
    U_j^{2p}r^{-2(p+k)}
    =(U_j/r)^{2p}r^{-2k}\leq1.
\]
The first term is one, giving the right bounds.

With right recovery from position $1$, the corresponding
matrix $G_{d-1}(t)$ gives
\[
    w^*=y^*G_{d-1}(t).
\]
The endpoint-extension proof established
$\|G_{d-1}(t)\|_2\leq B_d$.
This gives the left upper bound.
Nonvanishing follows from the extraction result,
and block extraction gives the lower bound.

The small endpoint uses this same construction for
the reversed polynomial, with dominant index $d-j$
and variable $s=\gamma_j/\lambda$.
Here $|s|\geq U_j$, so the preceding argument applies.
Pencil reversal multiplies the evaluated chart pencil
by a nonzero scalar and therefore leaves its
eigenvectors and recovery ratios unchanged.
head: environment

label: prop:exact-single-root-ratios
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:exact-single-root-ratios}
For every nonzero finite eigenvalue of $L_\alpha$,
the prescribed extractions are nonzero and
\[
    \rho_{\rm R}(v)=
    \begin{cases}
        f_{\rm C}(|\lambda|/\alpha),
            &0<|\lambda|\leq\alpha,\\
        f_{\rm C}(\alpha/|\lambda|),
            &|\lambda|\geq\alpha.
    \end{cases}
\]
Moreover,
\[
    1\leq\rho_{\rm R}(v)\leq\sqrt d,
    \qquad
    1\leq\rho_{\rm L}(w)\leq\widehat B_d.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The right formulas follow by adding the squared
block norms. Each sum contains $d$ terms bounded
by one and includes a term equal to one.

For either recovery rule, the left pencil eigenvector
satisfies $w^*=y^*G(t)$.
The proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:single-root-residual-amplification}
gives $\|G(t)\|_2\leq\widehat B_d$.
Thus $\|w\|_2\leq\widehat B_d\|y\|_2$.
The companion extraction results give nonvanishing,
and block extraction gives the lower bound.
head: environment

label: thm:exact-selected-ratios
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:exact-selected-ratios}
Let $\lambda\neq0$ belong to the assigned region
of a pencil in the linearization covering.
For every nonzero right and left pencil eigenvector,
the prescribed recovered vectors are nonzero and
\[
    1\leq\rho_{\rm R}(v)\leq\sqrt d.
\]
The left ratio satisfies
\[
    1\leq\rho_{\rm L}(w)\leq
    \begin{cases}
        B_d,&s\geq2,\\
        \widehat B_d,&s=1.
    \end{cases}
\]
In particular, $\widehat B_d$ is a common left bound
for every case.

The bounds include all region boundaries.
They require neither simple eigenvalues nor
invertible coefficient matrices.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The interior, endpoint, and single-root results cover
every assigned region.
Scaling preserves the pencil vectors, and reversal
changes an evaluated pencil only by a nonzero scalar
relative to its reversed chart.
Thus, the chart recovery ratios are also the ratios
for the original-variable pencils.

All arguments apply to every nonzero null vector,
without any simplicity or coefficient-invertibility
assumption. Finally, $B_d\leq\widehat B_d$.
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
For every pencil in the covering, at every nonzero
finite eigenvalue in its assigned region, the prescribed
recovery rules satisfy
\[
    \Gamma_{\rm R}(\lambda,v)\leq C_d,
    \qquad
    \Gamma_{\rm L}(\lambda,w)\leq C_d
\]
for all nonzero exact right and left pencil eigenvectors,
where
\[
    C_d=
    \begin{cases}
        A_dB_d\sqrt d, & s\geq2,\\
        A_d\widehat B_d\sqrt d, & s=1.
    \end{cases}
\]
In both cases, $C_d=O(d^{5/2})$.
head: environment
name: Backward-error amplification

title: Proof
body_md:
Combine the residual amplification bounds in
Section~6 with the recovery norm bounds in
Theorem~7.4.
head: environment
